Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Vignette:
Kofi's eyes still widen at the sound of a slammed door. It happens every time he's working late at the tax consulting firm, and a coworker bursts into the room without warning. He can't help but flinch, his mind racing back to that night two years ago when everything changed. The memory is fragmented, but certain images sear themselves into his brain: the feeling of being pinned down, the sound of his own muffled screams, and the taste of sweat and fear. That night, Kofi had been walking home from a party when he was grabbed by a stranger and pulled into an alleyway. The only sounds he remembers are the attacker's heavy breathing and the rustling of clothes as he struggled to free himself. When it was over, Kofi stumbled back to his apartment, locking the door behind him and collapsing onto the floor. In the months that followed, Kofi began to notice changes in himself. He would startle at unexpected touches – a tap on the shoulder or an accidental brush of hands in a crowded hallway. Simple interactions became fraught with anxiety as he found himself constantly assessing potential threats. Strangers approaching him on the street made his heart pound; being alone with men, even friends or family members, filled him with unease. As a result, Kofi started to curtail his social life, opting for solitary activities like gaming or watching movies in his room. His work suffered too, as he struggled to focus during client meetings, especially when male colleagues were present. He would scan the room for potential escape routes and mentally rehearse self-defense moves. The memories themselves came in waves, often triggered by seemingly innocuous stimuli – a door creaking open or the faint scent of cologne. Sometimes Kofi would relive the full intensity of that night without any visual cues; his heart racing, his senses on high alert. Other times, he'd taste the metallic tang of fear as if the event was unfolding all over again. His avoidance strategies became more entrenched as time passed. He stopped attending parties or going out with friends, afraid of being in unfamiliar places where danger might lurk around every corner. His apartment became his sanctuary, but even that felt precarious at times. When Kofi finally realized he needed help, it was after a particularly brutal flashback left him shaken for hours. He couldn't shake the feeling that he was living on borrowed time, waiting for the next trigger to send him spiraling back into that dark alleyway. His friends and family had been encouraging him to seek therapy, but Kofi had resisted, fearing that facing his fears would make things worse. Now, as he prepares to start therapy, Kofi's greatest fear is losing control – of his memories, his emotions, or himself. He hopes that by confronting the demons he's been avoiding for so long, he can begin to rebuild a sense of safety and trust in the world around him.
